questions.q: When 14 lines land in a reconciliation exception queue, what is the correct first step?
options: Sort them by reason, since different exception types require entirely different fixes
Assume all 14 are data errors and begin correcting them
Manually force-match all 14 to clear the queue
Increase the tolerance rule until all 14 disappear
questions.explain: The 14 lines broke down into three distinct categories (fees with no counterpart, outstanding checks, and amount mismatches), each requiring a different response.

questions.q: Why are the 3 outstanding check lines not actually a problem to fix?
options: Because outstanding checks should always be deleted
Because the bank already rejected those checks
Because they are a normal timing difference — checks issued and recorded, but not yet cleared by the bank
Because they represent duplicate entries
questions.explain: Outstanding checks remaining unreconciled until the bank clears them is expected and correct — 'not yet reconciled' is not the same thing as 'broken.'

questions.q: What was the root cause of one of the two genuine amount-mismatch exceptions?
options: The bank statement failed to load
A customer's wire amount was correct, but the receipt was keyed with transposed digits ($14,750 entered vs. $14,570 actual)
A duplicate receipt was entered
The period was closed
questions.explain: One mismatch was a straightforward data entry error — transposed digits between the amount keyed into the receipt and the actual wire amount.

questions.q: What is the correct way to handle a wire that arrived short due to an in-transit bank fee?
options: Ignore the shortfall and reconcile the mismatched amounts anyway
Ask the customer to resend the missing $200
Delete the receipt and start over
Record the fee as a separate bank charge and reconcile the net amount
questions.explain: Recording the in-transit fee as its own transaction allows the remaining amount to reconcile correctly against the receipt.

questions.q: Why does the resolution note explicitly separate the 14 lines into categories rather than describing them as '14 errors fixed'?
options: Because only 2 of the 14 were actual errors; the other 12 were normal, expected exceptions that don't represent a problem
To make the note look more detailed
Because Oracle requires categorized notes
Because the treasury analyst asked for a longer note
questions.explain: Documenting the categories accurately prevents a future reader from mistakenly believing all 14 lines represented data or system errors, when only 2 genuinely did.
